**Summary**

Sputnik 1 was the world’s first artificial satellite, launched on 4 October 1957 from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan (then the Soviet Union). “Sputnik” means “companion” in Russian. The idea of placing a satellite in low‑Earth orbit was first outlined in 1885 by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in *Dreams of Earth and Sky*.

Sputnik 1 was the first of a planned four‑satellite “Sputnik” series for the International Geophysical Year (1957‑58); three of the series (Sputnik 1, 2, 3) actually reached orbit. The spacecraft was a 58 cm‑diameter aluminum sphere equipped with four 2.4–2.9 m whip antennas that resembled whiskers. Inside a sealed capsule it carried transmitters operating at 20.005 MHz and 40.002 MHz (≈15 m and 7.5 m wavelengths) that emitted in 0.3‑second bursts. The satellite’s primary scientific goals were to measure the density of the upper atmosphere and to study radio‑signal propagation in the ionosphere; telemetry also reported internal and external temperatures.
